name: Burg Hasegg
kurzbeschreibung: Burg Hasegg in Hall in Tirol is the birthplace of the Thaler: imperial mint from 1567, roller press machine, and 46-metre M?nzerturm tower.
oeffnungszeiten: Sommer Di–So 10:00–17:00 Uhr, Winter Di–Sa 10:00–17:00 Uhr
beschreibung:
Overview

The sovereign castle Burg Hasegg is picturesquely situated on the southern edge of the historic old town of Hall in Tirol, approximately ten kilometres east of Innsbruck. The mighty fortification derives its name from the ancient field designation 'Eck am Hasenb?hel' and is revered as the birthplace of modern European currency history: starting in the 16th century, it housed the world-renowned Hall mint. Today, the complex attracts culture enthusiasts with the Museum M?nze Hall, the distinctive 46-metre-high M?nzerturm tower, and the late-Gothic St. George's Chapel.

History & Architecture

The castle was founded around 1300 by the Counts of Tyrol to protect the lucrative salt mines, the salt port, and the strategically vital crossing over the river Inn. Duke Friedrich IV. and Archduke Sigmund der M?nzreiche expanded the complex into a fortified residence. In 1494, Emperor Maximilian I. celebrated his wedding to Bianca Maria Sforza of Milan at Burg Hasegg; around 1490 he had commissioned the splendid St.-Georgs-Kapelle. The most globally significant milestone arrived in 1567: Archduke Ferdinand II moved the sovereign mint into Burg Hasegg. Here, the revolutionary roller minting press was invented, ushering in the mechanized mass minting of coinage worldwide. It was here that the Guldiner or Haller Taler was created?a coin whose name evolved in Bohemian Joachimsthal into 'Thaler' and ultimately into the global currency 'Dollar'. The twelve-sided M?nzerturm (constructed starting in 1477) rises 46 metres into the sky and stands as the unmistakable landmark of the salt-mining town of Hall.

Visit & Getting There

The museum and the M?nzerturm are open in summer (April to October) from Tuesday to Sunday, 10:00 to 17:00 (closed Mondays). In winter (November to March), M?nze Hall welcomes visitors from Tuesday to Saturday, 10:00 to 17:00 (closed Sundays and Mondays). Last admission is at 16:00. Admission prices for 2025/2026 for the combined ticket (Museum & M?nzerturm including audio guide): adults ?13.00, seniors and students ?11.00, children (6 to 16 years) ?9.00, family ticket ?28.00. Admission is free with the all-inclusive Innsbruck Card. Public transport: from Innsbruck Central Station via S-Bahn Tirol (lines S4, S5) in just 9 minutes to Hall in Tirol station, followed by an approx. 7-minute walk to the castle; alternatively take VVT bus lines 504 or 505 to the Unterer Stadtplatz or Stadtgraben stops. By car: via motorway A12, exit Hall Mitte, parking is available at the Altstadt underground car park or along the Stadtgraben.

Tips

The Museum M?nze Hall offers step-free wheelchair accessibility and audio guides (including an accessible text version for smartphones). Due to its 204 steep steps, the historic M?nzerturm is not wheelchair accessible, but those who make the climb are rewarded with magnificent 360-degree views over Hall and the dramatic rock faces of the Karwendel range. Inside the museum, visitors can use a traditional screw press to strike their very own tin coin as a unique keepsake.
